title: Launch HN: Versine (YC F26) – MCP to send and receive money
author: harshithl1777
summary: Hey HN, we’re Harshith, Param, and Vishnu and we're building Versine ( https://versine.com ). Versine lets you send and request money just by talking or texting with your AI (think Venmo with an MCP). We’re software engineers who have worked on distributed systems at Stripe, Databricks, and Amazon. Versine is an MCP that sits in front of a wallet with a balance. With it, your agent can do things like: - Send money to someone with your approval (via passkey in our app) - Send and request money to/from up to 100 people at once - Send money to people without a Versine account (they cash out to their bank in 2 mins) - Pay people without your explicit approval to trusted contacts (you can set this) Here’s a demo: https://youtube.com/shorts/Q9X7zioEqi0 We started working on this because assistants are frustratingly hands-off when it comes to finance and money movement. You can have your assistant go through a receipt and map out all the amounts owed taking care of splitting the subtotal, taxes, tips, but at the end of it the assistant hands back work to you when you have to go out and make the Venmo transfer. Our current solution is oriented towards power users: those who want to automate everything through their agent use us to split dinners, group trips, or settle poker ledgers. We see ourselves unlocking more value for the general consumer as 1. More people turn into power users of agents, and 2. We expand to a more complete banking solution: deposits, transfers, wires, everything you can (and more) do with your bank offered as an MCP. Behind the scenes, each user has a self-custodial stablecoin wallet storing USDC on Base. With self-custodial wallets, users own their keys, meaning money can’t be sent without their approval. Interestingly, we were almost forced into this solution because we had around 4 weeks to build this product (after a pivot), and traditional fiat with a partner bank would have caused far too many regulatory and compliance slowdowns. Because of that, the only fast option that remained was using stablecoin wallets. It also ensures we aren't a Money Services Business (MSB) since we don’t hold control or access to the user’s funds. Each call to the wallet creates what we call one-time or recurring standing permissions. For a one-time payment, your agent makes an MCP call, and you receive a notification in our mobile app. Once you swipe up in the app and approve with a passkey (or your device’s biometric method), we create a one-time permission that instructs your wallet to send $X to your recipient’s address. Trusted contacts let your agent send money to people that you’ve previously authorized without explicit passkey approval. Generally, these are people that you’d trust to send your money back even if your agent made a mistake. We’re also able to support sending money to someone off Versine using claim forwarding, where the user authorizes us to forward a specific amount to a future address (which we create once we verify a recipient's OTP). Param worked on scaling vector search at Databricks and harness evals at Glean. Harshith worked on core Stripe Connect fee-processing infrastructure and built an AWS Fargate autoscaler at Amazon. Vishnu worked on intent-based agent testing infrastructure at Amazon. None of us were experienced in stablecoin or crypto infra before working on Versine but our distributed systems experience has helped us a lot. We'd love for you guys to try it! It's available on iOS and Android and as an MCP on ChatGPT and Claude. We also support a public MCP and REST API for other agents. Please let us know how you find it and if it works as you'd hoped! https://versine.com Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50634426 Points: 34 # Comments: 14

title: How we built an open dataset of 309 Utah marketing agencies
author: Brand Captain
summary: We run a directory of Utah marketing agencies . This week we exported the data behind it as an open dataset: 309 agencies in 50 Utah cities, with services, team size, founding year and published rates. It's CC BY 4.0, and the CSV is on GitHub and Zenodo . This post covers how the list was built, what we cut before releasing it, and two problems we hit while publishing it. Step 1: collect candidates from four sources No single listing site has every agency, so we pulled candidates from four places: Clutch's Utah agency lists and profile pages DesignRush's Utah lists BBB search results for marketing and advertising businesses in Utah a hand-built list of agencies we already knew about Each source spells names and URLs differently. "Acme Digital", "Acme Digital LLC" and "acmedigital.com" are often the same company. We keyed every record on the website's domain and merged on that, falling back to the name only when a listing had no website. That gave us 507 candidates. Step 2: throw out what isn't a real Utah agency A script fetched every candidate's homepage and contact page, then dropped: Dead and parked domains. A regex looks for registrar pages and server errors: "is for sale", HugeDomains, "Website Expired", database errors, bad SSL. Listing sites keep profiles up after an agency closes, and this caught them. No Utah evidence. If neither the site nor any listing put the agency at a Utah address, it went. Agency lists for a state often include out-of-state firms. Video-only shops. Agencies that only appeared on video production lists, with no other marketing listing, were cut. Last, we searched Google Maps for each remaining agency by name and city. That added missing hours and contact details, and it dropped agencies Google marks as permanently closed. 309 made it through. Step 3: tag services from the agency's own words Services come from matching the agency's homepage text against fixed keyword lists for 13 categories: SEO, local SEO, web design, Google Ads, Meta ads, social media, branding, content, ecommerce, email, video, PR and full service. This has a clear limit, and we say so in the data card. If an agency runs Facebook ads but never says it on the homepage, it gets a 0 for Meta ads. Matching the site's own text kept the tags tied to what each agency says it does, not to what a listing site guessed. Each category is also its own 0/1 column ( svc_seo , svc_meta_ads and so on), so you can filter without splitting strings. Step 4: decide what not to publish The directory pages show more than the dataset does. Before releasing the export we dropped: "About" paragraphs copied from agency sites, because that text belongs to the agencies star ratings and review counts from Clutch, Google and BBB, because those belong to the platforms phone numbers and street addresses What's left is facts: name, city, website, services, team size band, founding year, minimum project size, hourly rate band, BBB accreditation, and the source listings for each row. Every row also links back to the directory, to its city page where one exists. Step 5: publish it where data people look The same files went to Zenodo (which gives it a DOI), Kaggle, DoltHub, GitHub and a Datawrapper chart. Two of those needed workarounds. DoltHub's CSV import failed. Dolt infers column types from the first rows and picked a short VARCHAR for the sources column. Rows with long source lists then failed to insert. The fix was to skip CSV import and upload a SQL file with the table created up front: CREATE TABLE agencies ( name TEXT , city TEXT , state TEXT , website TEXT , services TEXT , sources TEXT -- plus the svc_* columns and the rest ) ; INSERT INTO agencies VALUES ( . . . ) ; DoltHub opens the import as a pull request, so you merge it into main afterward. Datawrapper's API rejected our session. Calls to api.datawrapper.de returned 401 even while logged in. The app itself talks to the same API through /api/v3 on app.datawrapper.de , and that path works with the browser session. What's in the data A few numbers from the 309 rows: 70 agencies are in Salt Lake City, 35 in Lehi and 26 in Provo. Those three cities hold 42% of the list. 219 mention SEO on their homepage. Only 60 mention Meta or Facebook ads. Of the 275 agencies with a team size, 237 have fewer than 50 people. Of the 153 with a published hourly rate, 109 start at $100 an hour or more. Use it Browse by city and service: Utah marketing agency directory CSV and JSON: github.com/fedtman/utah-marketing-agencies Cite it: 10.5281/zenodo.24512883 If you spot an agency that's missing, closed or in the wrong city, open an issue on the GitHub repo and we'll fix it in the next refresh.

title: I Faked My Own Drug Valuation. 17 Lines of Python Caught Me.
author: Raymond Chang
summary: I build a drug valuation app called Somota. This week I tried to cheat on my own numbers, on camera, to see whether the app would catch me. Video: https://youtu.be/_qJZJFU8xTo The setup In a drug licensing deal, a valuation is usually a big spreadsheet that gets emailed between two companies, bankers and lawyers. Months later somebody asks which version everybody agreed on, and nobody can prove it. So every valuation in Somota is now signed as a receipt: Take every input (odds of success, costs, sales, discount rate) and serialize it as canonical JSON: sorted keys, no spaces. Hash it with SHA-256. That is the fingerprint. Sign the fingerprint with an Ed25519 key that never leaves my machine. Put the previous receipt's fingerprint inside the new one, so the receipts form a chain. What I tried Changed the odds of success from 10.8% to 30%. Caught. The fingerprint no longer matches, and Verify shows which field moved. Changed one character of the signature. Caught. The signature no longer verifies against my public key. Renamed receipt #2 so it vanished from the chain. Caught. Receipt #3 still points at the missing fingerprint. Deleted the newest receipt. Not caught. Nothing points at the newest receipt yet, so the chain still looks complete. That is a real hole, and the next thing I'm building (anchoring the latest fingerprint somewhere public) is meant to close it. The checker The other side of a deal shouldn't have to trust my software. This is the whole independent checker. It doesn't import anything from my app: # Check one Somota receipt without the Somota app. Usage: python check_receipt.py 1 import json , hashlib , sys from cryptography . hazmat . primitives . serialization import load_pem_public_key folder = sys . argv [ 2 ] if len ( sys . argv ) > 2 else "receipts" rec = json . load ( open ( f "{folder}/receipt_{int(sys.argv[1]):04d}.json" , encoding = "utf-8" ) ) body = { k : rec [ k ] for k in ( "n" , "issued_at" , "prev_hash" , "payload" ) } canon = json . dumps ( body , sort_keys = True , separators = ( "," , ":" ) , ensure_ascii = False ) . encode ( "utf-8" ) fingerprint = hashlib . sha256 ( canon ) . hexdigest ( ) print ( "Fingerprint matches:" , fingerprint == rec [ "hash" ] ) key = load_pem_public_key ( open ( f "{folder}/desk_public_key.pem" , "rb" ) . read ( ) ) try : key . verify ( bytes . fromhex ( rec [ "signature" ] ) , bytes . fromhex ( fingerprint ) ) print ( "Signature OK" ) except Exception : print ( "Signature FAILED" ) On a clean receipt it prints True and Signature OK . After I changed 10.8% to 30% it printed False and Signature FAILED . Note that it verifies the signature against the fingerprint it rebuilt itself, not against the hash field stored in the file. If you check against the stored field, a tampered file can still pass the signature step. What a receipt can't do If I sign garbage, the receipt just proves I signed garbage. It says nothing about where the inputs came from. It only answers one question: is this still the exact file that was signed? The harder problem is letting a buyer check my numbers without seeing all my data. That needs a different kind of math, and I'm working on it separately. How does your team prove a number never changed after everyone agreed on it?

title: I Built a Social App. Here is What I've learned About Real-Time Communication.
author: Oleksii Lyzen
summary: Introduction I've built this app to practice with WebSockets and Redis Pub/Sub . Basically, you create your account, log into it and you're welcomed with profile page. You can create a post, comment under a post, create/join room and talk in that room with its members. As a bonus, there's "friendship" feature that allows you to add/remove friends. Tech Stack I've already built few apps to practice my backend skills. I covered Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS deployment, pytest, etc. Real-Time Communication First Encounter First time when I needed to use WebSockets was when working with "Room" feature. When User opens any room, it fetches the messages. However, fetching them over and over again just to get messages(or nothing) - would be insufficient. Instead, WebSocket allows us to keep connection between Server and User open to use that to communicate between them. Implementation Issues As previously said, we can establish and keep the connection between User and Server using WebSockets. However, we expect our app to be used by more people than just one user. It creates certain problem that we have to solve: Sending messages to all users in scope of the room. Storing Connections Using FastAPI, we can get "WebSocket" object and store it. Each WebSocket needs a user its connected to. That means we can make our backend to store list of WebSockets to track them. When WebSocket disconnects - remove it, when connects - add. Since our connections scope is tied to room_id, I created dictionary "user_room_connections" user_room_connections : dict [ uuid . UUID , list [ WebSocket ] ] = { } Well, will that be enough? No, we also have to associate each WebSocket to each user. Unfortunately, they don't store any "user_id" that we can refer to. To create association, I created class "UserWebSocket". class UserWebSocket : def __init__ ( self , user_id : uuid . UUID , websocket : WebSocket ) : self . user_id = user_id self . websocket = websocket It contains user_id and WebSocket object. That way we can know which user connected to which WebSocket and vice versa. Now, thanks to that we can replace "WebSocket" with "UserWebSocker" in user_room_connection. user_room_connections : dict [ uuid . UUID , list [ UserWebSocket ] ] = { } That's it! Now we can send and receive messages in real time from any user who's in the same room as we... Or can we? Multiple Workers Problem Our previous solution works perfectly when we only have one Worker. What is Worker you ask? As I understand it, it's separate operating system process to handle user requests. They run independently from each other and so, they don't share any memory. We need more workers for better performance, scalability and reliability. Technically, it's possible to build communication pipeline between workers from scratch, however there's no need to do so since we already have working solution - Redis , and to be more precise, the Publish/Subscribe(Pub/Sub) features it allows us to use. Redis Introduction When it comes to Redis, it is important to understand that it exists as a separate service, meaning: we have to connect our FastAPI application to the Redis service in our code. Here's the way I did it: from redis . asyncio import Redis from backend . core . config import settings . . . async def lifespan ( app : FastAPI ) : redis = Redis ( host = settings . REDIS_HOST , # "localhost" port = settings . REDIS_PORT , # 6379 decode_responses = True ) . . . Additionally, it's worth to mention Docker, how useful it becomes when we have multiple services to work with and for establishing communication between them. Currently, our "REDIS_HOST" is set to "localhost" in "settings". You should change it to the name of your Redis service in your .env file whenever you run your application inside of a docker container. Publish/Subscribe(Pub/Sub) "Pub/Sub" is probably one of the most useful features that Redis gives us for dynamic communications between workers(workers don't know about each other's existence though). To begin, we first have to subscribe to the channel. # CHAT_EVENTS_CHANNEL = "chat:events" pubsub = redis . pubsub ( ) await pubsub . subscribe ( CHAT_EVENTS_CHANNEL ) Now, when our worker is subscribed, whenever user sends a message through a WebSocket, we can use that to publish message there. # CHAT_EVENTS_CHANNEL = "chat:events" await redis . publish ( CHAT_EVENTS_CHANNEL , "Hello, World!" ) The code here is overly simplified. There's more to "publish" than just raw line of text. In my final version of the app I use "RedisEvent" class to perform actions correspondingly to the event: class MessagePublic ( SQLModel ) : id : uuid . UUID content : str room_id : uuid . UUID sender_id : uuid . UUID | None created_at : datetime class RedisEvent ( SQLModel ) : event : Literal [ "message_created" , "message_updated" , "message_deleted" ] room_id : uuid . UUID message : MessagePublic | None = None message_id : uuid . UUID | None = None I then use "publih_chat_event" function to send the event. CHAT_EVENTS_CHANNEL = "chat:events" async def publish_chat_event ( redis : Redis , event : RedisEvent ) -> None : await redis . publish ( CHAT_EVENTS_CHANNEL , event . model_dump_json ( ) ) The decision behind "publish event" function is justified by the necessity of making not only receiving/sending messages dynamic, but also redacting/deleting them. I am sure there's better way to do this - it's something to find out for me next time. My First Impression it was my first time creating "Real-Time" communication using WebSockets and Redis service. I was very confused at first, but the more I used it the more I understood. Indeed. I enjoyed working on this project A LOT, especially the latter part. I never thought just how much it helps your site to look more alive and dynamic. I certainly want to experiment more with them in the future. What Next? I should mention that Redis has a lot more to it than just "Pub/Sub". There're still features to learn and experiment with. My next project will be all-in backend. I'll do my best to make it look professional so, even if there's no frontend, you still can learn a lot about project through clear documentation. Moreover, I want to deepen my understanding of the backend features I already use, improve my skills even more. Here's repo: https://github.com/futsu37/ChatNFriend

title: CVE-2026-119618 — Heap Corruption and RCE in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2
author: GUIDANCE WHITE
summary: At a glance Item Details CVE CVE-2026-119618 CWE CWE-362 (Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization) — per Apache. Red Hat classifies it as CWE-20 CVSS Red Hat/Amazon: 9.8 (Critical, CVSS 3.1) / CISA: 8.1 (High) — the Apache CNA record itself carries no score Affected component mod_http2 (bundled with httpd), and the standalone mod_h2 distribution on GitHub (archived since 2026-06-09) Affected versions httpd 2.4.55–2.4.70 / mod_h2 2.0.8–2.0.42 Fixed version httpd 2.4.71 (released 2026-11-11) Discovery Anthropic's OSS Scanner (automated report, 10/26) and Google Cloud Vulnerability Research (Anthony Weems, Simon Scannell, 11/3) — found independently, 8 days apart Public PoC googlesky/CVE-2026-119618 — reproduces heap corruption (use-after-free); no public RCE exploit A race condition in mod_http2 , Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, writes a header into the wrong table — one shared across the request instead of one private to it — and that mistake corrupts the heap. It triggers over unauthenticated HTTP/2 (h2 or h2c) traffic alone. Red Hat states that "a remote attacker could execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the httpd process." As of 2026-11-13, though, what's publicly demonstrated stops at heap corruption (a crash) — no public exploit has proven actual code execution yet. 1. Background — why HTTP/2 needs more than one thread HTTP/1.1 processes requests one at a time, in order, over a single connection. HTTP/2 multiplexes several streams concurrently over one TCP connection. To implement this, mod_http2 keeps request processing in a separate worker thread pool (H2Workers) , distinct from the connection thread. The connection thread reads and writes HTTP/2 frames and manages streams. Worker threads handle the actual request processing for each stream — these are mod_http2-specific threads that don't show up in mod_status and aren't counted against ThreadsPerChild . In other words, multiple worker threads run concurrently on top of a single HTTP/2 connection, processing requests in parallel. The trouble starts when that parallelism accidentally shares a data structure that was supposed to be private to one thread. 2. Root cause — a worker thread writing into a shared table Apache's own security advisory summarizes the flaw this way: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server's mod_http2 in assign_headers() can lead to RCE. Red Hat's analysis pins down the mechanism more precisely: a worker thread writes into memory owned by the connection thread through a shared, lock-free allocator. The function at the center of this is assign_headers() . When an HTTP/2 request ends with no body, carries a Content-Type header, but no Content-Length , mod_http2 needs to synthesize a zero-length Content-Length header and insert it. Before the fix, that synthesized header went into this table: /* vulnerable version (conceptually reconstructed) — assign_headers() */ if ( stream -> body_eos && r_type_present && ! content_length_present ) { /* req->headers: a table at the HTTP/2 request level, shared with — and potentially pooled alongside — other stream- or connection-level structures, not scoped to one request. */ apr_table_setn ( req -> headers , "Content-Length" , "0" ) ; } The patch changed exactly one line: /* patched version — assign_headers() */ if ( stream -> body_eos && r_type_present && ! content_length_present ) { /* r->headers_in: a per-request table, belonging only to the request_rec for this request. */ apr_table_setn ( r -> headers_in , "Content-Length" , "0" ) ; } req->headers is a structure multiple worker threads can reach concurrently; r->headers_in belongs exclusively to the one worker thread handling that specific request. The vulnerable version wrote to the shared table with no lock. When another worker thread, processing a different stream, touched the same structure at nearly the same moment — while the allocator underneath apr_table_setn was mid-reallocation — one thread would end up writing into memory that was already freed, or not yet initialized. The commit message itself gives no explanation (as Sysdig's researchers noted). The fix is a genuinely one-line change — but that single line touches the core concurrency question of "who owns this memory." Red Hat downgraded its own RHEL 9/10 builds from Critical to Important for a related reason: those builds allocate a separate allocator per HTTP/2 stream , which "substantially increases the complexity of exploiting the flaw." The same source-level defect carries very different real-world exploitability depending on how the memory allocator happens to be configured. 3. Trigger conditions — which requests reach this code path The public PoC ( googlesky/CVE-2026-119618 ) pinned down the trigger experimentally: A request that ends without a body and carries a Content-Type but no Content-Length triggers the bug. PUT / anything HTTP / 2 Content - Type : application / octet - stream < ends immediately with END_STREAM , no body > On receiving this, mod_http2 decides "there's a Content-Type but no body, so I need to synthesize Content-Length: 0" and enters the assign_headers() path. The request itself looks entirely ordinary — but firing this pattern across multiple concurrent streams on the same connection pushes worker threads into touching the same shared table at nearly the same instant, opening the race window. Reachability, laid out: Path Reachable? Notes Protocols includes h2 Yes HTTP/2 over TLS Protocols includes h2c Yes HTTP/2 over cleartext TCP — the path the public PoC targets Per-virtual-host Protocols Yes, for that vhost Check vhost blocks, not just the server-wide setting HTTP/1.1 only No Per Red Hat, servers serving only HTTP/1.1 aren't affected One easy trap: servers that upgraded to 2.4.67 back in May for an unrelated HTTP/2 flaw (CVE-2026-23918) are still squarely inside this CVE's affected range (2.4.55–2.4.70). Having recently patched an HTTP/2 bug does not mean you're safe from this one. 4. The patch — three commits, one line that matters The fix landed as three commits on the 2.4.x branch (824beab, 1b47e95, 5566851 — all on 2026-11-11). The core change, as shown above, swaps one table reference: req->headers → r->headers_in . What that swap actually buys: req->headers (vulnerable) r->headers_in (patched) Ownership scope HTTP/2 request-structure level — reachable from multiple worker threads request_rec level — exclusive to the worker thread handling that request Synchronization No explicit lock (relies on a lock-free allocator) No path for another thread to touch it concurrently Outcome Concurrent writes → allocator race → use-after-free The race condition has no way to occur Confirming the patch takes more than checking a version string. As Sysdig points out, distributions frequently backport fixes without bumping the upstream version number. # 1) The httpd version string itself (reference only — not trustworthy by distro) httpd -v # or apache2 -v # 2) The actually-loaded mod_http2 module version, per distro package rpm -q mod_http2 # RHEL/CentOS family dpkg -l | grep libapache2-mod-http2 # Debian/Ubuntu family # 3) Whether mod_http2 is even loaded (if it isn't, this CVE is moot) httpd -M 2 > /dev/null | grep http2 apache2ctl -M 2 > /dev/null | grep http2 A common false alarm in the field: Red Hat's Hardened Images httpd image is listed as "affected" per the vendor advisory, but the image doesn't actually ship mod_http2 at all — making it a case where the risk can simply be accepted. Don't panic off the version number alone — check whether the module is actually loaded first. 5. Affected versions and remediation Component Affected range Status httpd 2.4.55–2.4.70 Affected Upgrade to 2.4.71 httpd below 2.4.55 Not affected, per Apache's advisory No action needed for this CVE Standalone mod_h2 2.0.8–2.0.42 Affected Repository archived since 2026-06-09 — no fixed release will come. Switch to httpd 2.4.71's bundled module, or disable HTTP/2 RHEL 9 / 9.4 SAP / 9.6 EUS / 9.8 EUS Affected (Important) mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1 RHEL 10 / 10.0 EUS / 10.2 EUS Affected (Important) mod_http2-2.0.29-5.el10_3.1 RHEL 6 / 7 / 8 Not affected No action needed Debian 12 / 13 Patched 2.4.71-1~deb12u1 / 2.4.71-1~deb13u1 Ubuntu 22.04–26.10 Patched 11/12 security updates SUSE / openSUSE / Photon OS Waiting on vendor fix as of 2026-11-13 Track vendor advisories Immediate steps, where patching is possible Upgrade httpd on every server to 2.4.71 (or your distro's patched package) Restart httpd and rebuild images after patching — a running process keeps the old module loaded in memory. Bumping the package version without restarting leaves the server just as vulnerable If you're running standalone mod_h2 , switch to the module bundled with httpd 2.4.71 — the standalone repository is archived and will never get a fix Interim mitigation if patching isn't immediately possible Neither Apache's advisory nor the oss-security notice offers an official workaround, but Wiz recommends the following (note: this is Wiz's guidance, not Apache's): # httpd.conf (and identically in every VirtualHost block) Protocols http / 1.1 Remove h2 and h2c from the config entirely, leaving only HTTP/1.1 Apply this at the server level and in every VirtualHost block — many setups redefine Protocols per-vhost Restart or reload after the change Test latency-sensitive services first — clients fall back to HTTP/1.1, which can slow workloads that depend on multiplexing Containing the blast radius Run httpd workers as an unprivileged user, limiting what a compromised worker can read or write Keep secrets (API keys, DB credentials) in a secrets manager rather than environment variables or files the worker process can read directly From a detection standpoint Repeated segfaults in httpd child processes on an HTTP/2-enabled server — exactly the symptom the public PoC produces Since disclosure (11/11 onward), review httpd worker processes for shells, downloads, or unusual outbound connections Runtime detection tools like Falco/Sysdig can't see HTTP/2 frames directly, but post-exploitation steps — a shell spawned by a worker, a reverse shell, a downloaded binary executing, the web server process being replaced — were verified to be caught by existing rules with no modification One last thing worth noting: this bug lives entirely inside httpd's own HTTP/2 implementation, independent of whatever application code it's serving. No amount of hardening the application prevents it — patching is the only complete fix.

title: JavaScript: Build an Instant Quote Calculator With a Minimum Charge in Four Lines of HTML and Math.max
author: Robert Breen
summary:
A small office-cleaning business gets the same enquiry every day: "How much for our office?" Then an email back asking for the size, then a reply with a price a day later, by which time half the people have asked someone else. The pricing rule is simple: 12 cents a square foot, never less than $150. That rule fits in one line of JavaScript, and the whole calculator fits on one page. This post builds it in JSFiddle , the free code playground, with no account needed. What you build 2,000 square feet gives Estimate: $240.00 800 square feet gives Estimate: $150.00 (the minimum) Change the rate or the minimum and every quote follows. Step 1: The form (HTML panel) Four lines: a heading, a number box, a button and an empty paragraph for the result.

Office cleaning quote

The id values matter. They're how JavaScript finds each element. JSFiddle often adds closing tags for you as you type. If you end up with a doubled or a stray > , delete it. Click Run at the top. The Result panel shows the form. The button does nothing yet. Step 2: The price rule (JavaScript panel) Put the two numbers your price depends on at the top, as constants: const RATE = 0.12 ; // dollars per square foot const MINIMUM = 150 ; // smallest job we take Everything after // is a note for people; the browser ignores it. Now a function that prices a job: function quote ( sqft ) { return Math . max ( sqft * RATE , MINIMUM ) ; } Math.max returns the bigger of its arguments. For 2,000 square feet, 2000 * 0.12 is 240, which beats 150, so you get 240. For 800 square feet, 800 * 0.12 is 96, which loses to 150, so you get 150. No if statement needed; the minimum charge is built into one expression. Step 3: Connect the button Three lines find the page parts by their ids: const button = document . querySelector ( '#quote-btn' ) ; const box = document . querySelector ( '#sqft' ) ; const result = document . querySelector ( '#result' ) ; Then, when the button is clicked: read the box, price it, and write the estimate with two decimals. button . onclick = function ( ) { const price = quote ( Number ( box . value ) ) ; result . textContent = 'Estimate: $' + price . toFixed ( 2 ) ; } ; Two details: box.value is always a string , even in a number input. Number(...) turns it into a number before the multiplication. toFixed(2) turns 240 into "240.00" and 150 into "150.00" , so a price always shows cents. Point at the JavaScript panel and a small tidy icon appears at its top right. Click it and JSFiddle indents the code. Nothing changes in how it works; it's just easier to read. Step 4: Test both paths Click Run , then in the Result panel: Type 2000 and click Get my quote . You should see Estimate: $240.00 . Select the number, type 800 , and click Get my quote again. You should see Estimate: $150.00 . Always test one case on each side of the minimum. If the small office comes out at $96.00 , Math.max isn't in the path; if every quote is $150.00 , the box value probably isn't reaching quote() as a number. The full JavaScript const RATE = 0.12 ; // dollars per square foot const MINIMUM = 150 ; // smallest job we take function quote ( sqft ) { return Math . max ( sqft * RATE , MINIMUM ) ; } const button = document . querySelector ( '#quote-btn' ) ; const box = document . querySelector ( '#sqft' ) ; const result = document . querySelector ( '#result' ) ; button . onclick = function ( ) { const price = quote ( Number ( box . value ) ) ; result . textContent = 'Estimate: $' + price . toFixed ( 2 ) ; } ; Why this shape works Keeping the rule in one small function pays off as the pricing changes: The price lives in two constants. If the rate goes to 14 cents, you change RATE and nothing else. Nobody has to hunt through the click handler for a magic number. quote() knows nothing about the page. It takes a number and returns a number. You can test it in the browser console with quote(2000) and quote(800) without touching the form at all. The click handler only does wiring. Read the input, call the rule, write the output. If you later add a second input (say, visits per week), the handler grows by one line and the rule stays readable. That separation is the difference between a calculator you can maintain and one you're afraid to edit. Checklist [ ] Four HTML lines with ids sqft , quote-btn and result [ ] RATE and MINIMUM as constants at the top, so a price change is a one-line edit [ ] Math.max(sqft * RATE, MINIMUM) for the minimum charge [ ] Number(box.value) before doing math on the input [ ] toFixed(2) on the displayed price [ ] Tested above the minimum (2,000 → $240.00) and below it (800 → $150.00) The same HTML and JavaScript can go on a real website: whoever manages the site can paste both into a page. Practice it If you'd like to type it line by line with each step checked (13 steps, about 12 minutes, free), the interactive version is here: JavaScript: An Instant Quote Calculator for Your Website .

title: Can the business absorb a supplier price rise? The break-even math in integer cents
author: Tidy Cents
summary: A supplier email says "prices go up 8% next month". Turning that into a decision needs three numbers: the new monthly profit, the price rise that wins the old profit back, and the largest cost rise the business can take and still break even. Here is the arithmetic, in integer cents and basis points so nothing drifts. Inputs // all money in cents, all percentages in basis points (1% = 100 bp) const sales = 8_500_000 ; // $85,000 monthly sales const marginBp = 4200 ; // 42% gross margin const otherOut = 3_100_000 ; // $31,000 rent, payroll, software, loans... const directRiseBp = 800 ; // +8% on materials, stock, shipping const otherRiseBp = 500 ; // +5% on the other outflows Where the rise lands Direct costs and the other outflows react differently, so split them first: const pct = ( amount , bp ) => Math . round ( amount * bp / 10_000 ) ; const direct = sales - pct ( sales , marginBp ) ; // 4,930,000 = $49,300 const profitNow = sales - direct - otherOut ; // 470,000 = $4,700 const added = pct ( direct , directRiseBp ) + pct ( otherOut , otherRiseBp ) ; // 549,400 = $5,494 const profitAfter = profitNow - added ; // -79,400 = -$794 a month A $4,700 monthly profit becomes a $794 monthly loss. Nothing else changed. The price rise that wins it back Raising prices does not change what you pay per unit, so new sales must cover the new direct costs, the new other outflows and the old profit: const needed = direct + otherOut + added + profitNow ; // 9,049,400 = $90,494 // rise in basis points, rounded UP so it is never too small const priceRiseBp = Math . ceil ( ( needed - sales ) * 10_000 / sales ) ; // 647 bp = 6.47% This holds volume constant. If a price rise will cost you customers, the real number is higher, which is a reason to know the base case first. The largest rise you can survive If every cost rises by the same x, break-even is sales = (direct + otherOut) * (1 + x) : const maxRiseBp = Math . floor ( ( sales - direct - otherOut ) * 10_000 / ( direct + otherOut ) ) ; // 585 bp Round this one DOWN: a limit that is slightly too generous is worse than one that is slightly too strict. Why integer cents 0.1 + 0.2 problems are rare in one multiplication, but this chain has several percentages and a division; in floats the last digit of a cent-level result depends on the order of operations. With integers you round in exactly two places, on purpose, in the safe direction. If you want the same numbers without writing code, the free Cost Increase Calculator (FREE, no sign-up) shows them and how long the cash above your reserve lasts.

title: How I Built an 8-Language Shopify Store for LUVA Organic: hreflang, a 1px LCP Fix and AI Crawlers
author: Niya Mot
summary: Disclosure: I build and maintain the online store for LUVA Organic , a small hair, scalp and body care brand based in Ajman, United Arab Emirates. This is a write-up of client work. This post was generated with an AI writing tool from the store's theme code and live pages, and every technical detail below was checked against the live store on November 24, 2026. LUVA Organic sells a deliberately small collection: Phyto Elixir (a pre-wash hair oil), a shampoo, two scalp care products, Hair Mist Parfum (a fragrance for hair and skin, whose scent the brand describes as sophisticated, sweet and enveloping), Silk Skin (a body emulsion with the same scent) and a Ritual Pack. The store runs on Shopify with a custom theme, and the brief came down to four requirements: Eight languages, including right-to-left Arabic, plus Japanese, Korean and Russian. A fast first paint on phones. Consent that really gates analytics for visitors in Europe. Pages that search engines and AI assistants can read without guessing. Here's what worked, with the real snippets from the theme. 1. Eight locales, one URL prefix each, hreflang everywhere The store publishes eight locales: English (primary), Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean and Arabic. Each one lives in its own subfolder ( /es , /fr , /it , /ru , /ja , /ko , /ar ), and every page carries a full set of hreflang alternates plus x-default . The Hair Mist Parfum page , for example, points to /es/products/luva-hair-mist-parfum , /ja/products/luva-hair-mist-parfum and the other six versions. Arabic needs more than translated strings. The <html> element takes its language and direction from the request: {% - assign is_rtl = false - %} {% - if request . locale . iso_code contains 'ar' - %} {% - assign is_rtl = true - %} {% - endif - %} <html lang = "{{ request.locale.iso_code }}" dir = "{% if is_rtl %}rtl{% else %}ltr{% endif %}" > Language-specific fonts load only where they're needed: an Arabic font snippet for ar , and a separate snippet for ja , ko and ru . Visitors browsing in English never download them. 2. The 1-pixel LCP fix The home page opens with a full-screen photo. For a while, Lighthouse kept naming Shopify's cookie-banner text as the Largest Contentful Paint element. That text painted about a second after the photo, and mobile PageSpeed sat at 79. The cause: Chrome's LCP heuristics skip images that cover the entire viewport, because they look like backgrounds. On phones the hero was exactly one screen high, so the photo never qualified, and the next big thing on screen, the banner text, won. The fix is a single declaration: @media ( max-width : 767px ) { .hero-image { clip-path : inset ( 0 0 1px 0 ) ; } } Clipping the bottom pixel row means the image no longer covers the whole viewport, so it becomes the LCP element at first paint. Nothing is resized or moved, and the missing row sits under a dark shade where nobody notices it. The same rule now applies on tablets and desktops too, where the banner text had also been winning. 3. Preload the right hero for each screen The hero preload uses Shopify's CDN parameters on theme assets ( &width= and &quality= ), with a separate image for phones: <link rel = "preload" as = "image" fetchpriority = "high" media = "(max-width: 767px)" imagesrcset = "{{ hero_m }}&width=480&quality=85 480w, {{ hero_m }}&width=720&quality=85 720w, {{ hero_m }}&quality=85 958w" imagesizes = "100vw" > hero_m comes from asset_url , which already carries a ?v= query string, so the sizing parameters are appended with & . A matching preload with a (min-width: 768px) media query serves the desktop image, up to 2000px wide. 4. Critical CSS per template, the rest non-blocking The home, product and collection templates each inline their own critical CSS, and the full stylesheet loads without blocking the first paint: <style id = "luva-critical" > { % - case template .name - % } { % - when 'index' - % } { % - render 'luva-crit-index' - % } { % - when 'product' - % } { % - render 'luva-crit-product' - % } { % - when 'collection' - % } { % - render 'luva-crit-collection' - % } { % - endcase - % } </style> <link rel = "stylesheet" href = "{{ 'luva.css' | asset_url }}" media = "print" onload = "this.media='all'" > <noscript> {{ 'luva.css' | asset_url | stylesheet_tag }} </noscript> The three critical snippets are generated by a script that replays each template's first screen, and they're regenerated whenever the main stylesheet changes. Arabic pages and the theme editor keep the normal stylesheet load. Pruning unused rules also cut the main stylesheet by about 29%. In tests in October 2026, PageSpeed Insights scored the home page 100 on desktop and 95 to 98 on mobile on clean runs. Lab scores move from run to run, so read those as a range, not a promise. 5. Consent that actually gates analytics GA4 runs as a Shopify custom pixel instead of a hard-coded tag. The pixel receives the visitor's consent state, and visitors in Europe see a cookie banner first, so analytics only collects what each visitor has allowed. 6. Let AI assistants read the store More and more shoppers ask an assistant before they open a store. Three things help. Name the AI crawlers, but keep the default rules. The theme ships a robots.txt.liquid that keeps Shopify's default rules and adds the AI crawlers to the general group: {% - assign ai_agents = 'GPTBot,OAI-SearchBot,ChatGPT-User,ClaudeBot,Claude-SearchBot,Claude-User,PerplexityBot,Perplexity-User,Google-Extended,Applebot-Extended,Bingbot' | split : ',' - %} {% - for group in robots . default_groups - %} {% - capture block - %} {{ group . user_agent }} {% - if group . user_agent . value == '*' - %} {% - for agent in ai_agents %} User-agent: {{ agent }} {% - endfor - %} {% - endif - %} {% - for rule in group . rules %} {{ rule }} {% - endfor - %} {% - if group . sitemap != blank %} {{ group . sitemap }} {% - endif - %} {% - endcapture - %} {{ block }} {{ '' }} {% endfor %} Why not one group per bot? In robots.txt, a group that names a crawler replaces the * rules for that crawler. A lone User-agent: GPTBot plus Allow: / group would quietly reopen the cart, checkout and account paths for it. Listing the bots as extra user-agents in the general group gives them exactly the same rules as everyone else. Capturing each group first also keeps blank lines out of the middle of a group, which older parsers read as the end of it. Structured data on every page type. The home page outputs Organization , WebSite (with a SearchAction ) and FAQPage . Product pages output Product with Offer and Brand , plus a BreadcrumbList . Machine-readable instructions and categories. Shopify serves an agents.md file for the store (the same text is at /llms.txt ), and every product carries a category from Shopify's standard product taxonomy, which is what shopping agents and catalogs read. What I'd do again, and what I'd change Check which element is your LCP, not just the score. A decent score can hide the wrong LCP element. Name AI crawlers explicitly, but inside the default group, never in a group of their own. Settle the language list early. Adding a locale later is easy; changing URLs after launch means redirects. You can see the result at luvaorganic.com , or switch languages, for example to Spanish or Japanese . If you've hit the full-viewport LCP problem on another platform, I'd like to hear how you solved it in the comments.

title: Ratchet: A Closed-Loop Verification Gate That Turns PRDs into Live Browser Proof
author: Miracle Alajemba
summary: AI coding agents are great at writing code, but they love saying "it's done" the moment unit tests pass—without ever checking if the app actually works in a real browser. To fix that, I built Ratchet : a closed-loop verification gate powered by Kane CLI that refuses to lock a build until 100% of your PRD's acceptance criteria are proven in a live browser. How the Closed Loop Works Instead of relying on an agent's self-reported completion, Ratchet drives Kane CLI headlessly and enforces a strict verification flow: Spec Sync: Reads the project's PRD and syncs acceptance criteria against Kane CLI's structured design and coverage state ( kane-cli cover gaps --json ), including safe no-op handling when the design is already up to date. Live Browser Verification: Executes real browser tests via kane-cli testrun run against the running application (tested against a Pro Plan checkout demo with SAVE20 promo pricing). Evidence-Backed Lock: Parses Kane's coverage rollup and evidence packs, failing closed ( locked: false ) until every use case and acceptance criterion is proven. What Kane CLI Caught During the Build Wiring a real browser verification loop surfaced issues that standard unit tests would never catch: Sync Edge Cases: Caught a subtle mismatch where Kane's EMPTY_DESIGN event was treated as a hard failure when non-blocking clarification gaps were present, leading to a cleaner no-op sync path. Root-Cause Triage via Evidence Packs: Using kane-cli evidence serve , Kane separated real application behavior from test/environment noise—flagging a canonical trailing-slash URL assertion issue ( http://localhost:4173 vs http://localhost:4173/ ) and a transient screenshot timeout, confirming zero application bugs in the checkout flow. Run It Locally bash # 1. Install, build, and run offline engine tests npm install && npm run build && npm test # 2. Start the demo app (Terminal 1) cd demo-app && python3 -m http.server 4173 # 3. Run live browser verification and inspect coverage (Terminal 2) cd demo-app && kane-cli testrun run && kane-cli cover gaps --json Check out the code on GitHub: Miracle-Alajemba/ratchet

title: Find your break-even ROAS before you scale a single ad
author: Hermoso
summary: A campaign shows a ROAS of 2.4 and everyone is happy. Is it making money? Nobody can say from that number alone. A 2.4 ROAS is a fortune for a product that keeps 70% of its price and a slow leak for one that keeps 35%. The number that decides it is your break-even ROAS , and it takes five minutes to work out. Do it before you raise a budget, not after. If you want the answer without the sums, the free ROAS calculator does all of this in your browser and shows each formula next to its result. The rest of this post is the reasoning, so you can trust the number it gives you. What break-even ROAS means ROAS is revenue divided by ad spend. Spend $1,000, bring in $3,000, and ROAS is 3.0. Break-even ROAS is the ROAS where the money an order keeps exactly covers the ads that won it. Above it, the ads add profit. Below it, every sale they bring in costs you money, and scaling makes the hole deeper. There is a twin number worth knowing: break-even CPA , the most you can pay in ads to win one order and still end at $0. They are the same limit seen from two sides. One is in dollars per order, the other in revenue per ad dollar. Step 1: what one order keeps before ads Start with the price a customer pays for an average order and take away everything that order costs you, except ads: Product cost. What you paid to make or buy what is in the box. Shipping and fulfilment. Postage, packaging, pick and pack. Payment and platform fees. Card processing and any marketplace or store cut, usually a percentage of the price. Returns. The share of orders that come back, times the price. It is the cost people forget most often. What is left is the most one order can spend on ads. Call it what the order keeps. Step 2: the two break-even numbers Break-even CPA = what an order keeps before ads. Break-even ROAS = price ÷ what an order keeps before ads. That is the whole formula. Here it is on three real-looking shops. Example 1: a $60 skincare order Price $60. Product cost $18. Shipping $7. Payment fees 3%, so $1.80. Returns 5%, so $3.00. The order keeps $60 − $18 − $7 − $1.80 − $3.00 = $30.20 . Break-even CPA is $30.20. Break-even ROAS is $60 ÷ $30.20 = 1.99 . So the campaign at 2.4 is making money here, but not much: roughly 40 cents of revenue per ad dollar above the line. Example 2: a $45 apparel order with heavy returns Price $45. Product cost $14. Shipping $6. Fees 3%, so $1.35. Returns 25%, so $11.25. The order keeps $45 − $14 − $6 − $1.35 − $11.25 = $12.40 . Break-even ROAS is $45 ÷ $12.40 = 3.63 . The same 2.4 ROAS loses money on every sale here. The difference is almost all returns: at a 5% returns rate this order would keep $21.40 and break even at 2.10. Example 3: a $120 order with a thin margin Price $120. Product cost $80. Shipping $12. Fees 3%, so $3.60. Returns 10%, so $12.00. The order keeps $120 − $80 − $12 − $3.60 − $12 = $12.40 . Break-even ROAS is $120 ÷ $12.40 = 9.68 . A ROAS that high is hard to hold at any real volume, which tells you the problem lives in the price or the cost of goods, not in the ads. Order Keeps before ads Break-even CPA Break-even ROAS $60 skincare $30.20 $30.20 1.99 $45 apparel, 25% returns $12.40 $12.40 3.63 $120, thin margin $12.40 $12.40 9.68 Step 3: the ROAS you actually want Break-even means $0 of profit. To keep a margin, set it aside before the ads get their share. Take the margin as a share of the price: Target ROAS = price ÷ (what an order keeps − margin × price). For the $60 order and a 10% margin, the profit is $6 an order. That leaves $30.20 − $6 = $24.20 for ads, so the target CPA is $24.20 and the target ROAS is $60 ÷ $24.20 = 2.48 . The campaign at 2.4 sits just under that: profitable, but short of the margin you asked for. And sometimes the margin is out of reach. The $120 order keeps 10.3% of its price. It can never make a 15% margin, even if every visitor arrives for free. When the calculator says a target is not possible, that is the reason. Read it the way your ad platform writes it Platforms write ROAS in two styles. Google Ads uses a percentage: its Target ROAS help page turns $5 of sales per $1 of ad spend into a 500% target ROAS. Meta’s ROAS goal uses a multiple, and its example of $110 in purchases from a $100 budget, a 110% return, is entered as 1.100. So the skincare break-even is 1.99 in Meta terms and 199% in Google Ads terms. Same line, different notation. Two cautions about the ROAS the account shows you: It counts sales when they happen. A refund three weeks later does not come off it. That is why returns belong in your break-even, not in the platform number. It is the platform’s view of what it caused. Meta defines purchase ROAS as purchase conversion value divided by amount spent, and notes that statistical modelling may be used where some events cannot be counted directly. Compare it with the revenue in your store before you bet a budget on it. Check a campaign against the line Once you know what an order keeps, profit after ad spend is one line: revenue × contribution margin − ad spend, where the contribution margin is what an order keeps divided by the price. For the skincare shop that margin is $30.20 ÷ $60 = 50.3%. A campaign that spent $2,000 and brought in $5,400 kept $5,400 × 50.3% = $2,718, so it made $718 after ads. The same spend with $3,000 of revenue kept $1,510 and lost $490 , at a ROAS of 1.50. Both campaigns would look fine in a dashboard that only shows revenue. Before you scale, check these four things Use real costs. Pull product cost and shipping from invoices, not from the price list you set a year ago. Use your real returns rate. It moves the break-even more than anything else in apparel and footwear. Work each product on its own. A shop-wide average hides the item that loses money on every sale. Decide on repeat purchases on purpose. If customers reliably come back, you might accept a first order below break-even. That is a choice about lifetime value, and it should be written down, not discovered. Do it once, then let it run Put your numbers into the ROAS calculator and keep the break-even ROAS and CPA next to every campaign you run. Then, if you would rather not rebuild the spreadsheet every Monday, Hermoso is an AI marketing agent that runs your marketing on autopilot, and part of that is reading every ad platform you have connected to tell you what to scale, pause and test next , with the numbers behind each call. It never changes a campaign by itself. Questions people ask What is a good break-even ROAS? There is no universal good number, because it depends entirely on your costs. A product that keeps half its price before ads breaks even at 2.0. One that keeps a quarter breaks even at 4.0. Work out your own from price, product cost, shipping, fees and returns. How do I calculate break-even ROAS? Subtract product cost, shipping, payment fees and the cost of returns from the price to get what one order keeps before ads. Divide the price by that amount. A $60 order that keeps $30.20 breaks even at a ROAS of 1.99. Is break-even CPA the same as break-even ROAS? They describe the same limit. Break-even CPA is the most you can spend in ads per order, equal to what the order keeps before ads. Break-even ROAS is the price divided by that CPA. Should returns be included in break-even ROAS? Yes. Ad platforms record a sale when it happens and do not take refunds off later, so the returns have to be allowed for in your break-even instead. A 25% returns rate on a $45 order costs $11.25 per order. Originally published at hermoso.ai . title: How to use the Meta Ad Library (Facebook Ads Library): 2026 guide
author: Hermoso
summary: A real Meta Ad Library search in Hermoso: one brand's ads, each with its creative, copy and days running. The Meta Ad Library is the single most useful free tool in performance marketing, and most people use maybe a tenth of it. It's a public, searchable archive of every ad currently running across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and Threads, at facebook.com/ads/library, and plenty of people still call it the Facebook Ads Library. No login, no spend, no relationship with the advertiser required. Type a competitor's name and you see every active ad its page is running, with the number of results at the top. Type a keyword, in quotation marks for an exact phrase, and you see every advertiser whose ads use it. The catch is that the Ad Library shows you everything a page is running, with no ranking and no signal about what's working. Scroll a big advertiser and you'll see dozens of ads with no obvious way to tell the winners from the tests. This guide walks through how to search it properly, which filters actually matter, and the one reading trick (run-length) that turns an undifferentiated wall of ads into a ranked list of proven performers. Want the short version? Type a brand into our Meta Ad Library search and see its ads sorted by how long each one has been live, with the days counted for you. It needs a free Hermoso account, and each search uses a small amount of credits. How to search the Meta Ad Library Go to facebook.com/ads/library . Before you can search, the page asks you to pick a country and an ad category . Country matters. An advertiser's US ads and their UK ads can be completely different creative, so choose the market you actually care about. For category, leave it on "All ads" unless you're specifically researching housing, employment, credit, or political ads (those are archived under stricter rules and searched separately). From there you have two ways in: Search by advertiser (page). Type a brand name and select their verified page. This shows every active ad that page is running, which is the cleanest way to study one competitor end to end. Search by keyword. Type a term like "creatine gummies" or "project management" and Meta returns ads from any advertiser whose copy mentions it. This is how you discover competitors you didn't know you had, and how you find the best creative in a category regardless of who made it. Start with a known competitor by page to calibrate your eye, then switch to keyword search to widen the net. The keyword view is where the real discovery happens. You'll surface direct rivals, adjacent brands, and the occasional outsider running category-defining creative. The filters that actually matter Once results load, a handful of filters do most of the work: Platform. Filter to Instagram, Facebook, Messenger, or Threads to see where a competitor concentrates spend. A brand running almost everything on Instagram Reels is telling you where their audience is. Media type. Split image from video. If a category's top advertisers are overwhelmingly running video, that's a strong hint about what the platform is rewarding for that audience right now. Active vs inactive. The default view is active ads only, but you can view ads that have stopped running too. Inactive ads are a graveyard of tests that got cut, useful for seeing what a brand tried and abandoned. Date range / start date. Every ad card shows the date it started running. This is the most important number on the whole card, and the next section is entirely about why. What the Ad Library deliberately does not give you is any performance metric. There's no spend, no impressions and no click-through for standard commercial ads. So you can't sort by "best." You have to infer it. That's where run-length comes in. How to find winning ads for an app category There is no app category filter in the Meta Ad Library. You cannot pick "fitness apps" or "budgeting apps" from a menu, and the category picker on the first screen only separates ordinary ads from housing, employment, credit and political ones. You get to an app category in three steps instead. Search by keyword, with the category and the word "app". Try "budget app", "meditation app" or "language learning app". Keyword search matches the words in the ad copy, so it returns every advertiser describing itself that way, including apps you had not heard of. Keep the ads that send people to a store. An app install ad carries a button like "Install now", "Use app" or "Play game", and its link goes to the App Store or Google Play. Ads with those buttons are the app advertisers; the rest are articles, courses and agencies using the same words. Filter to video, then sort your attention by run-length. App advertisers lean heavily on short video, and the ad that has been live for months is the one the app is confident installs pay for. Open that advertiser's page to see everything else they run. Two other free libraries help here. TikTok's Creative Center has a Top Ads view that can be filtered by industry, which the Meta library cannot do. And the Google Ads Transparency Center shows the same advertiser's search and YouTube ads by domain. Hermoso's Ad Spy reads these libraries for you and ranks what it finds by how long each ad has run, and the app ad maker turns a winner into a version that shows your own app. Run-length: the free winner signal Here's the insight that changes how you read the entire library: how long an ad has been running is the closest thing to a public performance metric you'll get. Advertisers kill losers fast. If an ad isn't returning on spend, it gets paused within days. Nobody keeps paying to run creative that doesn't convert. So an ad that has been continuously active for weeks or months is, by revealed preference, an ad the advertiser is confident makes money. They've had every incentive to turn it off and chose not to. Longevity is the market voting with a budget. To read it, look at each ad's start date and do the subtraction against today. An ad that started three months ago and is still active is a proven winner in that account. An ad that started four days ago is a test. It might be great, but the brand doesn't know yet, and neither do you. When you're deciding which competitor ads to study and remix, sort your attention by run-length, not by whatever order Meta happens to show them in. The Meta Ad Library search does this subtraction for you and puts the longest runners first. A few honest caveats: run-length is a strong signal, not a certainty. Brand-awareness ads sometimes run long for reasons unrelated to direct response. Very large advertisers occasionally leave evergreen creative up out of inertia. And the Ad Library shows a start date but doesn't always make total run duration obvious at a glance across a big account. But as a free heuristic for "what is this brand confident about," nothing else in the tool comes close. If you take one habit from this guide, make it this: let the long-runners tell you what to copy. Turning what you find into your own ad Studying the library is step one. The gap most people never cross is going from "I found a great competitor ad" to "I have my own version of it running." Manually, that means screenshotting the ad, reverse-engineering its structure (the hook, the angle, the pacing, the CTA) and then briefing a designer or shooting your own creative around it. It works, but it's slow, and by the time you ship, the trend has moved. This is the part Hermoso automates. Its Ad Spy does the searching, filtering, and run-length reading for you: point it at a competitor or a category and it pulls their live ads from the Meta library (plus Google, LinkedIn, and organic TikTok), then ranks what it finds so the proven long-runners rise to the top instead of getting lost in the scroll. You skip the manual detective work and land straight on the ads worth learning from. From there you can remix. Hermoso's AI ad generator reads the structure of an ad you like and makes a version for your own product, with your brand, your product photo, your copy and CTA baked in, as an on-brand image or video ad ready to run. Under the hood it researches what's winning first, then routes across multiple top image and video models per job so you're never picking the tool. The free plan includes 165 free credits with no card required, so you can go from "I found a winner in the Ad Library" to "I have my own version" in one sitting. Try it on a competitor you already study , starting with the ad that's been running longest. Frequently asked Is the Meta Ad Library free to use? Yes. It's a public archive at facebook.com/ads/library with no login, no cost, and no relationship with the advertiser required. Anyone can search every ad running across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, and Threads in any country Meta operates in. Can I see how much a competitor is spending on their ads? Not for standard commercial ads. Meta only publishes spend and impression ranges for social-issue, electoral, and political ads. For everything else you infer performance indirectly, and the strongest free signal is how long an ad has been running. Why does how long an ad has run matter? Advertisers pause ads that don't return on spend, usually within days. So an ad that has stayed continuously active for weeks or months is, by revealed preference, one the advertiser is confident is profitable. They had every incentive to turn it off and didn't. Longevity is the closest thing to a public performance metric the Ad Library offers. How do I find competitors I don't already know about? Search by keyword instead of by page. Typing a category term returns ads from any advertiser whose copy mentions it, which surfaces direct rivals, adjacent brands, and outsiders running strong category creative you'd never have thought to look up. Can I filter the Meta Ad Library by app category? No. The library has no category filter for apps. Search by keyword with the category and the word "app", keep the ads whose button says "Install now", "Use app" or "Play game" and whose link goes to the App Store or Google Play, then rank them by how long they have been running. How does Hermoso use the Meta Ad Library? Hermoso's Ad Spy pulls a competitor's or category's live ads from the Meta library (plus Google, LinkedIn, and organic TikTok) and ranks them so the proven long-runners surface first. You can then remix any ad into an on-brand version for your own product, with your brand, product photo, copy, and CTA baked in. Is there a Meta Ad Library API? Yes, Meta offers an Ad Library API, but it only returns ads about social issues, elections or politics, and ads delivered in the EU. Ordinary commercial ads shown elsewhere are visible on the website but not through the API. Hermoso’s Meta Ad Library search reads a brand’s ads for you without either. Why can’t I find a brand in the Meta Ad Library? Usually one of four things: the brand advertises from a page with a different name (search its website or try keyword search), the country filter is set to a market it does not run ads in, it has no ads running right now, or its name collides with another page. Searching the brand’s website in Hermoso’s search avoids the name problem, because it matches the Instagram account the site links to. How long does the Meta Ad Library keep ads? Ads about social issues, elections or politics stay for seven years. Ads delivered in the EU stay for a year after they last ran. Other ads are shown while they are running, which is one more reason to note a winner when you see it. title: Fun-VACE redraw: the control video decides what transfers, and an 8-frame loop makes it long
author: AI-KSK
summary: Wan 2.2 Fun-VACE with an 8-frame overlap loop gives unbounded video redraw, and the controlling insight is that the control video you feed decides what transfers: pose video transfers pose, depth video transfers dynamics. Watch the episode: https://youtu.be/qX0N0DgZYAk Chinese original: https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1NNpczEE3Q The core mechanism Fun-VACE's redraw behaviour is determined by the control signal, not by the prompt. That is a cleaner mental model than prompt-based control: Feed an extracted pose video: the output follows the pose. Feed a depth video: the output follows the dynamics and volume. The reference is optional - it supplies style or identity, not motion. Why the 8-frame overlap Long redraw is done in windows. Overlapping eight frames between windows keeps the seam continuous, which is what makes a minute-long redraw look like one shot instead of a series of clips. Dual control The episode covers pose and depth control together - two control streams constraining the same generation. In practice that means a shot can hold a specific body configuration and a specific spatial structure at once. What to check Pose transfer versus depth transfer on the same source - do they really produce different results, as claimed? The window seam at frame 8 boundaries, watched closely. Long runs: does the style drift, even if the pose holds? Where this sits among the VACE episodes Other episodes cover VACE with Lynx identity, VACE with audio, and VACE inside merges. This one is the plainest and most useful: control video in, redraw out, looped. Honest limits Control quality dominates: a bad pose or depth extraction becomes a bad redraw, unfixably. Unbounded loops still accumulate drift. No workflow or weights are bundled with this article.
